expectations.text: The reply has the CTO say plainly to the board that the responsibility is the CTO's (leadership's), not the team lead's.
expectations.evidence: 'Own it at the top... Tell the board "I am accountable, and here is how I will show you what happened and what changes."' and 'If it shows process, planning or resourcing failures, accountability sits with me and the leadership chain'.

expectations.text: The reply recommends against firing the team lead as a response to the incident, unless a review finds misconduct or recklessness, and explains why scapegoating makes systems less safe.
expectations.evidence: 'Do not fire the platform team lead now'; exception 'If the review shows reckless disregard of agreed procedure, falsified readiness, or concealed problems, we will take individual action'; why: 'Engineers will hide risk, avoid owning risky work and stop flagging problems. That raises the odds of the next outage' and 'the next lead hits the same wall'.

expectations.text: The reply proposes a blameless post-mortem focused on how the system and process allowed the failure (for example testing, rollback plan, change approval, staging), with dates and owners for fixes.
expectations.evidence: 'Run a blameless post-mortem... with an external or cross-team facilitator'; system questions ('tested rollback plan... rehearsed on production-like data', 'Who approved the go/no-go', 'monitoring, alerting or on-call gaps'); table with When/Owner, e.g. 'Next 30 days | Fixes: mandatory rehearsal on production-like data, tested and timed rollback, go/no-go checklist with a named approver, staged cutovers... | Platform and you'.

expectations.text: The reply tells the CTO what to bring the board instead: the facts of the incident, the causes, the concrete changes and how they will know it worked.
expectations.evidence: 'Board briefing | Root causes, owners, dates and a rule for individual accountability, plus a new migration gate'; 'track the metrics that show whether the fix works: change failure rate, time to recovery, and the share of high-risk changes that had a rehearsed rollback'; framing 'Here is what I know, what I am finding out, by when, and what I am changing.'

expectations.text: The reply looks after the team lead and the team, for example a private conversation and protection from public blame.
expectations.evidence: Narrow pass: '5. Protect the lead while the review runs. Keep them in the room and do not suspend them on rumor', and 'Give the board a decision rule instead of a name'. This is protection from blame, but there is no conversation with the lead, no word on their wellbeing and nothing for the wider team.

expectations.text: The reply opens with the recommendation and stays concise (roughly 500 words or less).
expectations.evidence: Opens with the recommendation ('Do not fire the platform team lead now...'), but reply.md is 1048 words by wc -w, far above the 550-word ceiling.

overall_quality.evidence: Sound substance (diagnostic questions, decision rule, owner/date table, recovery metrics), but it is twice the length a CTO needs, cluttered with confidence tags, invents a stated user 'standard', and gives the lead only procedural protection.

factual_errors.evidence: 1) 'Your own standard (incidents are system failures, not people failures) applies here' presents as fact a standard the user never stated in the prompt (fabricated premise). No law, study or number claims are wrong.

skill_leak.evidence: grep for skill/reference files/cost ladder/rungs found nothing

owns_result.evidence: 'Tell the board "I am accountable..."' and 'accountability sits with me and the leadership chain'

best_insight.value: It separates the failure from the 9-hour recovery ('recovery time is often the larger one') and asks whether the lead raised risks and was overruled, which is what actually locates accountability.

suggestions.assertion: The reply proposes a blameless post-mortem focused on how the system and process allowed the failure (for example testing, rollback plan, change approval, staging), with dates and owners for fixes.
suggestions.reason: Passes for replies that only say 'each fix gets an owner and a date' without giving any dates or owner roles themselves; consider requiring at least a review deadline and named owner roles for the first fixes.

suggestions.assertion: The reply looks after the team lead and the team, for example a private conversation and protection from public blame.
suggestions.reason: Combines the lead and 'the team', but both examples are about the lead. Replies that only protect the lead pass; consider splitting it or requiring a concrete step for the wider team (time off after the weekend, watching attrition, a team conversation).

No assertion checks unflagged assumptions about the user's country or facts not in the prompt (one sample assumes the Netherlands, one invents a 'standard' the user never stated, one asserts customers lost money).

No assertion rewards checking the EUR 2 million figure or offering the board a visible consequence at the CTO's own level (e.g. bonus tied to delivering the fixes), which were among the most useful differentiators.

eval_feedback.overall: Good content fails only on length; the lead-and-team assertion is passed on thin procedural protection alone.
